column1: What is the size and visual angle of the fovea centralis, and how many letter spaces does this correspond to at normal reading distance?
column2: The fovea centralis is ~1.5mm in diameter, subtending ~2 degrees of visual angle, corresponding to approximately 4-5 letter spaces at 14-16 inches reading distance.

column1: How does visual acuity degrade at 10 degrees and 20 degrees from the point of fixation?
column2: At 10 degrees from fixation, acuity falls to roughly 25% of foveal performance; at 20 degrees, it approaches legal blindness by clinical standards.

column1: What is the functional difference between parafoveal and peripheral vision in reading?
column2: Parafoveal vision (5 degrees either side of fixation) provides enough resolution for word shape/length/initial-letter preview benefits, but cannot support full letter-level word identification. Peripheral vision (beyond 10 degrees) contributes almost nothing except gross spatial/line awareness.

column1: What physiological parameter remains constant (20-40ms) regardless of reading distance, and what does it represent?
column2: Saccade duration remains relatively constant at 20-40 milliseconds regardless of distance, representing the minimum refractory period of the extraocular muscles.

column1: State the core invariant governing the speed-comprehension tradeoff in reading.
column2: The speed-comprehension tradeoff is a hard cognitive law rooted in finite working memory capacity (3-4 chunks) and the sequential nature of language processing—you cannot arbitrarily accelerate one cognitive stage without creating pressure on the others, analogous to pouring five gallons into a three-gallon bucket faster.

column1: What are the two possible consequences when reading speed is pushed beyond working memory's processing capacity?
column2: Either information begins dropping (reducing comprehension), or the reader employs cognitive shortcuts that bypass deep semantic processing.

column1: Break down the ~200-250ms fixation duration during untrained reading into its two components.
column2: Roughly 100 milliseconds for the saccadic eye movement itself, and another 150 milliseconds for cognitive processing and meaning extraction.

column1: Given 4 fixations per second with single-word recognition, what is the hard ceiling on reading throughput, and why?
column2: Maximum throughput cannot exceed 240 words per minute under ideal conditions, because each fixation typically processes only one word and the eye is functionally blind during ballistic saccadic jumps.

column1: What are the three mechanical bottlenecks that accelerated reading training attacks simultaneously?
column2: 1) Expanding effective recognition span via perceptual chunking (multi-word units), 2) Eliminating regression behavior through forward momentum discipline, 3) Reducing fixation duration through tempo conditioning.

column1: What is the cardinal invariant of expert reading that conventional speed-reading instruction ignores?
column2: Reading velocity must subordinate itself to purpose—expert readers modulate cognitive investment dynamically based on material complexity, informational density, prior knowledge, and use case, rather than maximizing speed universally.

column1: How do System 1 and System 2 processing map onto speed reading versus deep analytical reading?
column2: Speed reading techniques exploit System 1 (fast, parallel, pattern-matching: peripheral vision, chunk recognition, predictive inference). Deep analytical reading demands System 2 (slow, serial, deliberative: propositional integration, critical evaluation, counterfactual reasoning).

column1: What formula defines the 'efficiency index' used as the primary optimization target in speed reading training, and why is it used instead of raw WPM?
column2: Efficiency Index = Speed (WPM) × Comprehension (%). It is used instead of raw WPM because it penalizes speed increases that degrade understanding, preventing comprehension sacrifice for velocity gains.
